Spent the day on Capitol Hill, which always leaves me with a brackish mix of hope over what we can be and despair over how far we are from our potential. Remember that we plant seeds today for trees whose shade we will not enjoy.

It's impossible to avoid the economic effects of mass deportation. A new analysis in Choices Magazine breaks down what aggressive enforcement could mean for American workers, farmers, and your grocery bill. 🧵

Combined across agriculture, construction, hospitality, and other sectors, mass deportations affecting millions of workers could fuel inflation and reduce GDP, effects felt by every American household, not just immigrant communities.

The data is clear: undocumented workers are deeply embedded in the U.S. economy. Policy decisions that ignore this reality carry real costs.

Something remarkable happened this week: a Substack post helped expose and remove the first-ever ICE 287(g) enforcement agreement with a K-12 school district in the United States. Here's what we know. 🧵
The signed agreement has been removed, but the actual document has not been made public. A public records request will likely be needed to see what was signed. This story is not over.

Andrew Thrasher's full account of how this unfolded (the questions that remain, and what it means for schools) is essential reading. This is what independent, data-driven accountability journalism looks like in 2026.

The deeper issue: the Caney Valley school district police force was created only 8 months ago. It was a brand new agency, and within months it had nearly deputized its officers with federal immigration enforcement authority over a school serving children.

That explanation raises serious questions. Signing a federal contract is not how you gather information. The MOA is a detailed, multi-page document. ICE's own website even has a section titled "How Can I Convince My Chief or Sheriff to Participate in 287(g)?"

The district's explanation: Police Chief Michael Coates signed the multi-page Memorandum of Agreement while trying to "gather more information" about a training program. The superintendent said Coates was surprised to learn he had actually enrolled.

The removal came after local journalists began asking questions prompted by Thrasher's post. Andrew and I discussed the implications in real time on Substack Live. This is exactly the kind of rapid, collaborative public accountability work that matters right now.

The Caney Valley Public Schools Police Department in Washington County, Oklahoma had a signed Task Force Model 287(g) agreement approved by ICE on March 13, 2026. It appeared on ICE's official spreadsheet then was quietly removed two days later.

That explosive growth includes 17 Florida college campus police departments, 600+ sheriffs' offices, state highway patrols, and even fish and wildlife agencies. But last Monday, Andrew Thrasher spotted something new: a K-12 school district.

The 287(g) program allows ICE to deputize local law enforcement with federal immigration enforcement authority. Since Jan. 20, 2025, the program has grown from 134 active agreements to over 1,530, nearly 11x increase in just 14 months.

Conflicting accounts over whether the school's police chief actually signed the paperwork, whether he was tricked into signing it, and why ICE is approving K-12 school districts – including elementary schools – in it's enforcement program raise red flags.

After Andrew, several reporters, and I looked more closely, it was clear that the school district was no longer enrolled in 287(g). But the story doesn't stop there. Reporter's accounts and statements by the school's superintendent and police chief only added confusion.
